lessons.title: A game coin balance
lessons.summary: Store 20 starting coins and 7 spent coins. Calculate and print the coins left.
explanation: A program is a list of instructions the computer follows. A value is one piece of information, such as the number 30 or the text "coins". Numbers have no quotation marks here. Quotation marks tell JavaScript that the characters inside are text, also called a string. This project uses numbers so it can subtract an amount spent from an amount available.

A variable gives a value a name. In `const savedCoins = 30;`, `const` creates a name that cannot later be assigned a different value. `savedCoins` is the name, and the single equals sign `=` assigns the value on its right. A name cannot contain spaces or begin with a digit. JavaScript distinguishes capital and small letters: `savedCoins` and `savedcoins` are different names. The semicolon ends this instruction.

`console.log()` is a function used to display information. A function is a reusable action; calling it asks it to run. The dot in `console.log` selects the `log` action belonging to `console`. Parentheses `()` contain the value you want to display. Put the variable name inside, without quotes, to display its value. `console.log("coinsLeft")` instead displays the literal word coinsLeft because the quotes make it text.

Assignment and comparison ask different things. `const balance = 22;` assigns a value. `balance === 22` asks whether the value is exactly equal to 22 and produces `true` or `false`. Those are Boolean values, the two possible answers to a yes-or-no question. The minus sign subtracts; the plus sign adds numbers; the star `*` multiplies numbers. Choose the sign that matches the action you mean.

For your project, calculate with the supplied variable names so the calculation follows their values. The supplied amounts give 20 minus 7, which is 13. A second run with spending changed to 5 gives 15. Trace each line: which two values go into the expression, what number comes out, and which name is printed? Storing a number and displaying it are separate steps, and the checks look at both.

analogy.familiar: A labeled place on a score sheet
analogy.connection: The name helps you refer to the current number.
analogy.limit: A variable is not always a separate box in computer memory. Objects can be shared through names, and const prevents reassignment of the name but does not freeze every object value.

lessons.title: A temperature checker
lessons.summary: Keep the supplied temperature at 24 and comfort limit at 22.
explanation: A type is the kind of value you have. JavaScript uses numbers for calculations, strings for text, and Booleans for yes-or-no results. `17` is a number; `"17"` is a string containing two characters. `true` and `false` have no quotes because they are Boolean values. A comparison checks how two values relate and produces one of these Booleans.

The signs `<` and `>` mean less than and greater than. The signs `<=` and `>=` include equality too: less than or equal to, and greater than or equal to. `===` is strict equality, which compares without changing the values' types. A single `=` assigns a value. Use assignment to store the answer from a comparison, such as `const below = temperature < limit;`.

Strict equality also checks the type. `"19" === 19` is false because text and a number are different kinds of values. `19 === 19` is true. Automatically changing one type into another is called coercion. JavaScript has comparison forms that allow coercion, but `===` avoids it. Keep temperatures and limits numeric here; do not add quotation marks to them just because they will be displayed later.

You can reason about each answer without running code. Put the two numbers on a number line, then ask the question written by the sign. In the exercise, 24 lies to the right of 22: below is false, equality is false, and above is true. `24 >= 22` is also true. With a value of 21 and a limit of 22, below becomes true. These are separate questions, not three steps that alter the temperature.

Check three cases: a value below the limit, exactly at the limit, and above the limit. Each comparison should agree with the case. Printing the named answers in order lets you see which question each result answers. The stored Booleans are actual values, so `above === true` checks that the above comparison produced true. An output string saying "true" and the Boolean `true` are different values even though they may look alike on screen.

analogy.familiar: Checking a thermometer against a mark on a wall.
analogy.connection: Comparison operators tell the program which side of the mark a number falls on.
analogy.limit: A Boolean reports true or false; it does not explain why the temperature has that value.

steps: Keep the supplied temperature at 24 and comfort limit at 22.
Complete the three comparisons for below, at, and above the limit.
Print the three true-or-false results in this order: below, atLimit, above.
Try a value equal to the limit and observe which comparison is true.

checks.label: String and number differ under strict equality

quiz.question: What is `14 >= 18`?
quiz.explanation: 14 is neither greater than nor equal to 18, so this comparison produces the Boolean false.

lessons.title: Choose a game difficulty
lessons.summary: Keep the setting as `"medium"`.
explanation: Sometimes the next action depends on a value. A condition is a question that produces true or false. An `if` statement checks a condition and runs its block only when the answer is true. A block is code grouped inside braces `{}`. An `else if` supplies another question when the earlier one was false, and a final `else` handles anything still unmatched.

The setting is a string, so compare it with quoted text using strict equality `===`. Exact spelling matters: `"easy"` and `"Easy"` are different strings. Declare a message with `let` because your branches will assign its selected value afterward. Unlike `const`, `let` allows reassignment. `let message = "";` starts with an empty string, which contains no characters.

An if/else chain selects at most one branch. After one branch runs, JavaScript skips the later branches in that chain. Parentheses after `if` and `else if` contain the condition; braces contain the action. An `else` has no condition because it covers the remaining possibilities. A semicolon ends each assignment, while a closing brace ends its block.

Your project needs three known settings, so give easy, medium, and hard their own comparisons. The expected messages are "Take your time", "Ready for a challenge", and "Expert mode". The final else should assign "Unknown setting". With the supplied medium value, the easy test fails and the medium test succeeds. With hard, the first two tests fail and the third succeeds.

This exercise assigns and prints a message; it does not need `return` because its code is outside a function. If you see a short branch such as `if (condition) message = "text";`, JavaScript allows a single statement without braces. Braces make the grouping easier to see and let you safely add another statement. Try each setting, then an unknown one, and predict which block runs before reading the output.

analogy.familiar: A signpost with several labeled paths and a final “other path” sign.
analogy.connection: Each condition selects a message for one setting; the last branch catches unrecognized values.
analogy.limit: Branches are checked in order, so an earlier true condition prevents later branches from running.

lessons.title: A countdown display
lessons.summary: Create an empty `countdown` array.
explanation: A loop repeats a block of instructions. One trip through the block is an iteration. A countdown needs three decisions: where the number starts, when another iteration is allowed, and how the number changes afterward. A `for` loop places these three parts inside parentheses. The code inside braces is called its body.

Read `for (let n = 4; n >= 1; n--)` as: start n at 4; keep going while n is at least 1; decrease n by 1 after each body. The two semicolons inside the header separate these parts. They are part of the loop syntax, not instructions to remove. `n--` is a short way of subtracting one from n. The update happens after the body, before the next condition check.

Trace the stopping point carefully. At n = 1 the condition `n >= 1` is true, so 1 is added. The update makes n = 0. Now the condition is false, and the loop stops. It never adds 0. Four values were added. `.length` is the number of array entries, and square brackets read one entry by its index, which starts at 0. For four entries, the last index is 3.

Every repeat must move toward stopping. If you start above 1 but increase n instead of decreasing it, `n >= 1` can stay true forever. A missing update can cause the same problem. This is called an infinite loop. Write the start, condition, and update together, then mentally follow at least two iterations and the final condition check.

For the required countdown, start at 5 and include 1. The five visited numbers are 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Store them in `countdown`, then print the joined result. Its length should be 5; indexes 0 and 4 hold 5 and 1. In checks, `&&` means both questions must be true, such as checking the first and last entry together. Counting values and counting array indexes are different: five entries occupy indexes 0 through 4.

analogy.familiar: Calling out numbers as someone walks down five steps.
analogy.connection: The counter moves down one step each time through the loop.
analogy.limit: A loop repeats code; it does not automatically know when a countdown should end.

steps: Create an empty `countdown` array.
Use a for loop to count down from 5 to 1, including both numbers.
Use .push() to add each number to the end of countdown.
Print the array and check it has exactly five values.

quiz.explanation: It visits 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, and 2: six values. The condition includes 2; the next value, 1, fails it.

hints: Create the array before the loop.

math.feedback: The outputs are 4, 3, 2, and 1: four lines. The endpoint 1 is included; 0 is not.

lessons.title: A packing list
lessons.summary: Start with the three supplied items.
explanation: An array is an ordered list of values. Write square brackets `[]` around its entries and commas between them. Strings inside the array still need quotes. `const tools = ["pencil", "ruler"];` creates two string entries in order. The array can grow or change while keeping the same name.

An index is an entry's position. JavaScript starts indexes at zero: the first entry is at 0, the second at 1, and the third at 2. Reading `tools[0]` gets the first entry. The brackets after a name mean read at this position; brackets in a declaration create the array. `.length` gives the count of entries, which is not the last index.

`.push()` is an array method: a function belonging to an array. Call it with the new item inside parentheses. It changes the existing array by adding at the end. The word mutable means changeable. An array is mutable. A `const` declaration prevents assigning a completely different array to that name, but it does not prevent adding or updating entries in the current array.

An empty array has length 0 and no final entry. With an ordinary nonempty list, last index equals length minus one. Asking for an index that has no entry produces `undefined` rather than a real packed item. Be careful with `list[list.length]`: for a three-entry array it asks for index 3, which is one past the final existing entry.

Your supplied packing array begins with shirt, book, and snack. Add the exact string "water bottle" with push. The length changes from 3 to 4, the new final entry is water bottle, and the first entry remains shirt. Printing the final entry and length together uses two arguments separated by a comma.

analogy.connection: The array keeps the order; push adds the next entry and length counts entries.
analogy.limit: An array index is a position starting at zero, while length is a count starting at one for the first item.

lessons.title: A reusable distance converter
lessons.summary: Write `convertDistance(distance, factor)`.
explanation: A function packages steps so you can use them again with different inputs. Defining a function describes the steps; calling it runs them. The definition begins with `function`, followed by its name, parentheses for input names, and braces around the body. A converter multiplies the distance by a conversion factor, a number that tells you how much to scale it.

A parameter is a name for an input inside the function. An argument is the actual value supplied by the calling code. In `function scale(value, factor)`, value and factor are parameters. In `scale(4, 3)`, 4 and 3 are arguments. Commas separate inputs. Their order matters: the first argument fills the first parameter and the second fills the second.

Returning and displaying are separate actions. `return 6;` makes the caller receive 6; it does not put 6 on screen. `console.log(6);` displays 6; it does not make a function return 6. A function with no return value returns `undefined`. Keep the converter's calculation in its return so other code and the checks can use the result, even without displaying it.

The project function is named `convertDistance` and needs the two supplied parameters. Return their product. The checks call your function directly with zero and with several other distances and factors. For 3 and 2, the product is 6; for 5 and 1.6, it is 8. Using the parameters rather than returning a fixed number makes all these calls work.

A conversion factor includes a meaning, such as destination units per original unit. Keep that direction in mind: multiplication uses the factor supplied for this lesson. Multiplying by the factor converts the distance but does not edit an outside variable that held the original number. You can inspect a returned value by placing the call inside `console.log(...)`; the inner call finishes first, then its result becomes the argument of the display function.

analogy.familiar: A recipe that takes an amount and gives back a converted amount.
analogy.connection: The function receives a value and factor, multiplies them, then returns the answer.
analogy.limit: Returning a result does not print it; display is a separate action.

steps: Write `convertDistance(distance, factor)`.
Multiply distance by factor and return the result.
Try convertDistance with inputs (0, 2), (3, 2), and (5, 1.6).
Print one result and check the other returned values.
lessons.solution:
function convertDistance(distance, factor) { return distance * factor; }
console.log(convertDistance(3, 2));

quiz.explanation: return passes a value back to the caller. Displaying that value requires a separate printing operation.

lessons.title: A game character card
lessons.summary: Create the hero with name, health, and equipment fields.
explanation: An object groups related values under property names. A property pairs a name with a value. Write braces `{}` around an object, a colon `:` between each property name and value, and commas between properties. One character object can hold text for its name, a number for its health, and an array for its equipment.

Dot notation reads a named property. `character.health` means get the health property of character. Add `= 9` to replace that property's value. This assignment targets one property; it does not replace the whole object. To read an item inside an array property, combine dot notation with an index, such as `character.equipment[0]`.

Objects are mutable, which means their contents can change. Declaring the variable with `const` keeps the name attached to this object; it does not freeze the properties. `character.health = 9;` is allowed. Trying to assign a different whole object to `character` is not allowed after a const declaration. These are different operations.

Property spelling matters just like variable spelling. `health` and `Health` refer to different properties. Reading an absent property normally gives `undefined`. Keep related information in one object but be precise about which field an instruction changes. If you wanted subtraction, you would write an expression such as `character.health = character.health - 3;`, which reads the current value before assigning the new one.

In the exercise, hero already contains Mira, health 10, and lantern equipment. Assign 7 to hero's health property, then read the existing name and equipment. The checks compare all three results so you can see that the targeted update worked. Think of the colon as pairing a property during creation and the equals sign as assigning a value afterward.

analogy.familiar: A character card with labeled spaces for name, health, and gear.
analogy.connection: Property names label the separate details stored together.
analogy.limit: Objects can contain nested values and shared references; changing one property does not automatically copy the whole object.

quiz.explanation: The assignment targets the health property only. Coins remains 4, and the old health is replaced by 9.

lessons.title: A flexible greeting tool
lessons.summary: Write two functions that return different greetings for a name.
explanation: A function is also a value in JavaScript. You can give it a name, pass it as an argument, and let another function call it. A function received this way is called a callback. A higher-order function is one that receives or returns a function. These names describe what the code does; there is no extra magic syntax needed to pass a callback.

Distinguish the function from its result. `friendly` means the function itself. `friendly("Noor")` calls it immediately and means the value it returns. If a receiving function expects something it can call, pass the function name without parentheses. Its parameter can then hold that function value and call it with an input.

Backticks make a template literal, a string that can insert values. Inside it, `${name}` evaluates name and adds its value to the text. The dollar sign and braces mark the insertion; ordinary quoted strings do not perform this insertion. Function parentheses contain inputs, function braces contain instructions, and template-literal braces surround an expression to insert. Their meaning comes from where they appear.

The exercise also puts returned greetings on a page. In a browser, `document` represents the page. `document.querySelector("#g1")` finds the element with id g1; the `#` marks an id in this selector string. Assigning its `.textContent` sets its plain text. That requires the supplied HTML elements to exist. It does not treat the greeting as HTML instructions, so angle brackets in text stay text.

Your two supplied callbacks are friendly and playful. Pass each to showGreeting with Ari to obtain the expected two different messages. Store each result, then assign it to the matching page element's textContent. These callbacks run when showGreeting calls them; a callback can also be saved and called later in other designs. The browser elements are practice fixtures, while the main skill is passing a function and using its returned value.

analogy.familiar: Handing a friend one of two greeting cards and asking them to read it aloud.
analogy.connection: The wrapper receives a greeting function and uses the text it returns.
analogy.limit: Passing a function gives code the ability to call it; it does not run automatically at the moment it is passed.

steps: Write two functions that return different greetings for a name.
Inside showGreeting(makeGreeting, name), run makeGreeting with name and return the greeting it gives back.

lessons.title: A cleaner score report
lessons.summary: Use the supplied player object with name and score.
explanation: You can make a readable sentence from information stored in an object. An object groups named properties, such as a player's name and score. Destructuring is a short way to read several properties into variables at once. It saves repeated property reads; it does not convert numbers into text or create a live connection to later changes.

Read `const { name, score } = player;` as: read player.name into name, and player.score into score. The property names inside the braces must match the source object. Here the braces are a destructuring pattern, not a new object. `const` means each extracted variable cannot be reassigned. For numeric and string properties, you receive their current values.

Template literals use backticks rather than ordinary quotation marks. `${...}` marks a place where JavaScript evaluates an expression and includes its result in the string. The dollar sign starts the insertion and the braces contain the expression. Text outside the braces stays as written, including spaces and punctuation. Numbers are represented as text in the resulting sentence without changing the original number variable.

Keep names precise. A missing property yields undefined, so a misspelled destructuring name can put undefined into a report. A single equals sign assigns the extracted values; `===` compares values. Destructuring an object property that is itself an object shares that object's reference, but the exercise extracts only a string and a number. For those values, later replacing player.score does not update the extracted score variable.

Your supplied player is Kai with 18 points. Extract name and score, then use both in the expected sentence and preserve its period. The check also confirms score remains the number 18. For the math example, the expression 4 + 2 inside `${}` evaluates to 6 before the surrounding text becomes `Score: 6`. First identify the inserted expressions, evaluate them, and only then read the finished sentence.

analogy.familiar: Filling labeled blanks on a score card.
analogy.connection: Destructuring picks named fields; the template fills those details into one report.
analogy.limit: Destructuring does not validate that a property exists; missing values can still be undefined.

lessons.title: A workout summary
lessons.summary: Use the supplied minutes `[20, 35, 45]` and keep sessions of 30 minutes or more.
explanation: Processing a list often takes three steps: select some entries, transform the selected entries, and combine their values. An array method is a function attached to an array. `filter` selects, `map` transforms, and `reduce` combines. Each receives a callback, a function it calls for individual entries. This project selects long sessions, converts their minutes to seconds, and calculates a total and average.

An arrow function is another way to write a function. `m => m >= 30` means take an input called m and return the comparison. With two inputs, use parentheses: `(sum, x) => sum + x`. The arrow `=>` introduces the function body; it is different from `>=`, which compares numbers. For a short expression body, the arrow function returns that expression automatically.

Reduce carries an accumulated answer from one entry to the next. `seconds.reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0)` starts sum at 0, then adds each x. The comma and final 0 provide the initial value; they are not another array entry. For 1800 and 2400 the running answers are 1800 and 4200. Starting at zero also gives an empty list the total 0.

The expression `condition ? a : b` is a conditional expression: use a when the condition is true, otherwise b. Here a nonzero length counts as true; a zero length counts as false. Divide total by the number of kept sessions using `/`. With no kept sessions, an average has no value, so return `null`, JavaScript's explicit no-value marker. Do not divide by zero or pretend an empty average is zero.

For the exercise list, 20 is removed and 35 and 45 remain. Their seconds are 2100 and 2700, total 4800, average 2400. An average in minutes for 30 and 50 is their sum 80 divided by 2, or 40. Use the count of the selected list, not the original list, and keep the unit consistent throughout each calculation.

analogy.familiar: Sorting workout slips, converting each duration, then adding them.
analogy.connection: Filter selects sessions; map changes values; reduce totals them.
analogy.limit: An average for zero items is undefined by the usual formula, so the program needs a deliberate empty result.

Convert kept minutes to seconds with `map`.
Calculate total seconds and average seconds.
Return zero total and null average for an empty list.

quiz.question: Keep only durations of 30 or more from [15, 30, 50, 25]. How many remain?
quiz.explanation: 30 and 50 meet the inclusive threshold. 15 and 25 do not, so two values remain.

hints: Filter before converting: keep values at least 30.
Convert each kept minute value to seconds by multiplying by 60.

math.question: Two selected activities take 20 and 40 minutes. What is their average duration?
math.feedback: Add the selected durations, then divide by their count: (20 + 40) / 2 = 30 minutes. The total alone is not the average.

lessons.title: A live character editor
lessons.summary: Read the name and color from the supplied inputs.
explanation: A web page contains elements such as inputs, paragraphs, and buttons. In browser JavaScript, `document` gives access to the page. `document.querySelector("#name")` finds its first element with id name. The `#` means an id selector; the quotation marks make the selector text. This method can return null when nothing matches, so this exercise supplies matching HTML before your script runs.

An input element's `.value` is the text currently in its field. A paragraph's `.textContent` controls its visible plain text. They serve different purposes: read value from an input and write textContent to the preview. `.style.color` controls its text color, using a valid color string such as "purple". The dot selects each named property; assigning with `=` changes that property.

Use this HTML as the page for the following browser example. ```html

``` Each id names one element for JavaScript to find. The input value attributes provide starting text. The paragraph begins empty. This is page markup, not JavaScript; place it in an HTML page and run the next script after these elements exist.

An event is something that happens on the page. The input event fires as a user edits a field. lessons.title: A reaction timer

explanation: A timestamp records when something happened. JavaScript's `Date.now()` gives a timestamp measured in milliseconds since a fixed reference date. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second. To measure a duration, subtract the earlier timestamp from the later one. The result is elapsed time, not a clock reading. Both numbers must use the same unit and reference.

The program needs state: stored information that can change between actions. Use let for the saved start and elapsed values. `null` means there is no recorded value yet. Use null rather than 0 as the missing marker because zero can be a valid timestamp or duration. A signal saves a starting time; a later click can calculate the difference.

`!==` means strict inequality: are these values different? The guard allows calculation only when startedAt is different from null. An early click must be ignored because no signal time exists. `Math.max(a, b)` chooses the larger number. Taking the maximum of 0 and the difference prevents a negative duration when supplied times are out of order. It cannot turn a bad clock reading into a reliable measurement.

In a real browser button, a click event listener can call `clickAt(Date.now())` when clicked. The signal action would call `signal(Date.now())` at its starting moment. Starting a new signal should clear the previous elapsed result; reset should clear the start too. A timing measurement from this simple clock is a practice estimate, and real applications may use a monotonic clock for durations that must ignore wall-clock adjustments.

lessons.title: A data-loading card
lessons.summary: Create `loadCard(fetchData)` as an async function.
explanation: Some work finishes later, such as obtaining data. A Promise represents an eventual result. It can be pending while unfinished, fulfilled with a value, or rejected with a reason. A rejection means that operation failed. A Promise is not the data itself, so code must wait for the result before using it as loaded data.

An `async` function always returns a Promise. Inside it, `await` pauses that function until a Promise settles. It lets other work proceed while waiting; it does not freeze the whole browser. If the Promise fulfills, await produces its value. If it rejects, await throws the rejection so a surrounding catch block can handle it.

The try block contains work that can fail. A catch block receives the thrown error when that happens; error.message is its explanatory text. `new Error("Offline")` creates an error object. The function parameter getData is a callback: the loader calls it to start the supplied work. `Promise.resolve(value)` creates a fulfilled Promise; `Promise.reject(error)` creates a rejected one.

Represent each stage explicitly: idle before loading, loading while waiting, success with data, and error with a message. This gives a page enough information to show the right card. Object shorthand `{ status: "success", data }` means the data property holds the variable data. This exercise stores these states in an object; displaying a real card would read that object and update page elements.

In your project, showSuccess and showError create the final states, and loadCard sets loading before calling and awaiting fetchData. Store the returned Promise as successfulLoad. `instanceof Promise` checks whether an object is a Promise; it does not prove success or verify the final displayed data. The checks exercise the state helpers too. Use an awaited demo to inspect a completed load; reading state immediately after starting a load can still see loading.

analogy.connection: The Promise settles later, and the card switches from loading to success or error.
analogy.limit: This lesson uses supplied Promise scenarios; a real network request can fail, take longer, or return invalid data.

Its parameters receive the supplied values. `this` refers to the instance whose method is running. Assigning `this.health = health` puts the input number into that particular object's health property.

Damage subtracts from the current health. `Math.max(0, difference)` chooses whichever is larger, ensuring health does not fall below zero. This lower bound is inclusive, so zero is permitted. Without the maximum, taking 20 damage from 14 health would produce -6. This rule applies to nonnegative damage amounts as supplied; negative damage would increase health, so a larger application would define and validate its allowed inputs.

The method changes a property and does not return the updated health. Inspect `.health` after calling it. This differs from a pure converter function that returns a new number without editing an object. `const fern` is allowed because the name stays attached to the instance even while its properties change. lessons.title: A route search game
lessons.summary: Use the supplied graph with start A and target F.
explanation: A graph describes places and their connections. A node is one place; an edge is one connection. An adjacency list records each node's neighbors, such as `{ P: ["Q", "R"] }`. A path lists nodes traveled through. Four nodes along one path have three edges because an edge joins each consecutive pair. This lesson searches for a path to a target node.

Breadth-first search, or BFS, visits nearby nodes before farther ones. Its queue stores discovered nodes waiting to be processed. A queue takes the oldest added entry first: push adds at the end of an array and shift removes its first entry. Each queue entry can hold the node and its path. A Set records seen nodes; it keeps each name only once and supports has and add.

`while (queue.length)` repeats while the queue has entries. Destructuring `[node, path]` reads the two parts removed by shift. `visited++` increases the count by one. `graph[node]` reads neighbors using a variable as a property key. `|| []` supplies an empty array if the lookup is missing. The for/of loop visits each neighbor. `!seen.has(next)` means the node has not already been seen. The spread `...path` copies the path's entries into a new array before adding next.

In an unweighted graph, every edge counts equally, so BFS finds a path with the fewest edges. When two paths tie, neighbor order decides which is discovered first. Seen nodes prevent endless revisits around cycles, where connections lead back to earlier places. Marking a node when adding it to the queue avoids adding it repeatedly. If the queue empties without reaching the target, return null for the path and the measured visit count.

The exercise graph's BFS tie is resolved by its neighbor order, producing A-B-D-F: four nodes, three edges. All six reachable nodes may be visited before F is processed. A missing target Z returns path null. Compare approaches on the same graph and state what you counted; a visit count on one graph does not prove one search is always faster. Array shift and path copies also cost work, so visits are a useful measure here rather than a complete benchmark.

analogy.connection: BFS explores by distance layers; DFS explores one path deeply.

lessons.title: A responsive search tool
lessons.summary: Increase `latestId` each time a search starts.
explanation: A search can start before an earlier search finishes. Responses may arrive in the opposite order from their requests. If an old response is displayed just because it arrived last, it can replace the answer the user currently wants. A request id is a number assigned when a request starts; keep the largest, newest id so the program can identify current work.

Use let for the newest id and the visible text because they change. Start the id at zero, then use `latestId++` to add one for each search. A Set holds canceled ids without duplicates. `.add(id)` records one, and `.has(id)` checks membership. Marking an old id canceled is bookkeeping in this fixture; it does not stop a real network operation.

The guard contains two questions joined by `&&`, meaning both must be true. The strict equality asks whether the result belongs to the newest id. The exclamation mark `!` means not, so `!cancelledIds.has(id)` asks whether it has not been canceled. The function only assigns visibleResult inside this guard. A stale result leaves the current text alone.

For real browser fetch work, an AbortController can request cancellation. Create a controller, pass its `.signal` in fetch's options, and call `.abort()` when the work becomes outdated. The request can reject with an abort error. Cancellation may arrive after completion, and stopping the client does not prove the server did no work. Keep the id guard as well. The supplied exercise models cancellation using a set rather than making actual fetch calls.

In your exercise, oldId must be smaller than newId. Mark oldId canceled when starting the new request, display "new answer", and ignore "old answer" even when it arrives afterward. Arrival time does not change which request is current. Tests should vary response order and confirm that stale text never overwrites current text. The canceled-id set grows in this small fixture; a long-running application could remove entries once the old work can no longer return.

analogy.connection: A request number marks which result is current.

lessons.title: A tested data-processing tool
lessons.summary: Require an array containing only finite nonnegative numbers.
explanation: A robust function states what input it accepts and what it does for invalid input. This total function accepts an array of finite, nonnegative numbers. Finite means a normal bounded number rather than Infinity or NaN, which means not a number. Nonnegative includes zero. Text such as "4" is not a numeric input even though it looks like a number.

Validate before summing. `Array.isArray(values)` checks the whole input shape. `.some(callback)` reports whether at least one entry fails a rule. `typeof v` tells you the kind of value; compare it with "number". `Number.isFinite(v)` checks for a finite numeric value without converting text. `||` means at least one condition is true, and `!` means not. These let you reject a non-array or an invalid entry.

`throw` stops normal processing and sends an error to the caller. `new TypeError(message)` makes an error object that describes a wrong input kind. A caller can use try/catch to handle it. This is different from returning an error-looking string, which could accidentally be used as if it were the total. Valid inputs return numbers; invalid ones throw an explicit error.

A test supplies an input and compares behavior with an expected outcome. Cover ordinary values, an empty list, zero, negative values, numeric-looking text, non-array input, Infinity, and NaN. A large valid array checks that all entries are processed. `Array(10000).fill(1)` creates ten thousand entries containing 1, so its expected total is 10000. Tests should inspect results and errors rather than requiring a particular spelling of the code.

The exercise checks total 5 for [2, 3], zero for empty input, clear TypeErrors for negative and text entries, and 10000 for the large list. The math total of 2, 3, and 5 is 10. Ordinary array tests do not prove every possible input works: this simple contract assumes dense arrays containing only the described values. JavaScript numbers also have finite precision, so very large sums can need additional range or precision decisions in a real application.

explanation: Several people can request the same supply. A grouped total combines rows with the same item name. The input is an array of objects; each object has item and quantity. The ?? operator chooses its right-hand value when its left-hand value is null or undefined. For a missing item, counts.get(item) ?? 0 gives you a starting total of zero. This also preserves an existing zero. A for...of loop can then visit every request exactly once.

Map treats ordinary strings such as "constructor" as ordinary keys. This avoids the special inherited properties found on a plain object. Names are compared exactly here: "Pen" and "pen" are separate items. The requirements do not ask you to clean names, so do not silently merge them.

lessons.title: A task board that keeps its old copy
lessons.summary: Write toggleTask(tasks, id). Return a new array; copy the matching task with done reversed. Leave all other task objects and the original array unchanged. IDs are unique strings. If the ID is missing, return a new array with the same task objects.
explanation: A task board may need its old state for undo or comparison. Mutation means changing an existing value in place. An immutable update creates the changed parts as new values and keeps the old state intact. This project practices that pattern with an array of task objects.

An array contains references to objects. Copying the array with [...tasks] creates a new array, but its task objects are still shared. Changing copied[0].done would also affect the object seen through tasks[0]. To change one task safely, create a new object for that task too.

map calls a function for each array item and builds a new array from the returned values. Return a new object for the matching ID. Return the existing task for other IDs: unchanged objects can be shared safely because your function does not edit them. Preserve task order.

This is a shallow copy: nested objects would still be shared unless you copy the nested part you change. Our tasks contain an ID, a Boolean done value and optional other properties. Keep those properties with object spread. The function assumes unique IDs, so a single requested ID refers to at most one task.

Check four cases: an unfinished task becomes finished, a finished task becomes unfinished, a missing ID leaves values alone, and an empty list remains empty. All cases return a fresh array. Compare the original after each call: preserving its data is part of success, not just getting the new checkbox value right.

analogy.limit: Object spread is shallow, so nested data may still be shared.

lessons.title: A note editor with reversible history
lessons.summary: Write createHistory(initial), where notes are strings. Return methods current(), edit(text), undo(), redo(). Each method returns the current string. Undo/redo stop at the ends. Editing after undo discards the redo branch; editing the current text does nothing.
explanation: Undo needs more than the current note: it needs previous versions and a position within them. Model the editor with an array of strings and an index called a cursor. An invariant is a fact that must stay true: the cursor always points to an existing version, and current() returns that version.

A closure is a function that keeps access to variables from where it was created. createHistory can create versions and cursor, then return methods that share those variables. Each call to createHistory gets its own storage. The caller can operate the editor without directly changing its internal array.

Undo moves the cursor left if an earlier version exists. Redo moves it right if a later version exists. Neither action changes the array. At the first or last version, return the current text unchanged. Avoid negative indexes or reading past the final entry.

If the new text equals the current text, return immediately. A repeated edit should not create a duplicate undo step or remove a useful redo branch. Strings suit this exercise because callers cannot mutate a saved string in place. Saving arbitrary objects would require a clear copy or immutability policy.

Test sequences, not just isolated methods: edit A to B to C, undo to B, then edit D. Redo must remain D because C belongs to the abandoned branch. Also test an empty string, repeated undo at the beginning, duplicate edits and two independent histories. Those transitions expose mistakes a single happy path would miss.

analogy.familiar: A row of saved note cards with a marker on the current one
analogy.connection: Undo moves the marker; a new edit after undo replaces the cards ahead of it.
analogy.limit: Real editors may group keystrokes and limit history size; this exercise treats each edit call as one version.

steps: Inside createHistory, keep the saved versions and a cursor that points to the current version.
Return an object with current, edit, undo, and redo methods.
Do not let undo go before the first version or redo go past the last version.
If you undo and then make a new edit, remove the later versions from the old history.
Ignore an edit if its text is the same as the current text.
Create two histories and check that changing one does not change the other.

quiz.explanation: The new edit discards the old future version Final. Revised is now the latest version, so redo stays there.
